segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Okay, let's get into it. This is the postmortem for the outage on the ingestion pipeline last night. Dimitri, you were on call, can you walk us through the timeline first?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Sure. At ten fourteen PM I got paged for elevated error rates on the event ingestion service, jumped from our normal zero point one percent to about eighteen percent within a few minutes.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: Eighteen percent is huge, that's basically one in five events failing.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Right, and it kept climbing. By ten twenty two it hit forty three percent, which is when I escalated and paged Kenji since it looked like it was on the ingestion service he maintains.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: I got paged at ten twenty four, was already half asleep, sorry for the slow initial response, took me about six minutes to get to a laptop.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: That's a reasonable response time honestly, no need to apologize.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: By ten thirty we were at full outage, basically zero events processing successfully. That lasted until we identified the root cause at eleven oh five.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: So thirty five minutes of full outage plus about sixteen minutes of degraded service before that. What actually caused it?

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: The root cause was a deployment earlier that evening, around nine forty five, that included a schema change to the events table, adding a new required field for the funnel builder work.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: The migration itself succeeded, but the deploy didn't account for a backlog of queued events still using the old schema without that field.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Right, so as the queue drained, every event missing the new required field got rejected by validation, which is why the error rate climbed gradually instead of spiking immediately, it was proportional to how much of the backlog was old format versus new.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: So this was a backward compatibility miss on the schema migration.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Exactly. I should have made the field optional with a default value for at least one deploy cycle before enforcing it as required.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: How did we actually fix it once identified?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Kenji pushed a hotfix making the field optional again at eleven oh two, and error rates dropped back to normal by eleven ten.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: The hotfix was fast because it was a one line change, the hard part was actually finding the root cause, we spent most of that thirty five minutes looking at the wrong thing initially.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: What was the wrong thing you looked at first?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: We initially suspected the database itself, since we'd had that disk space issue on staging a couple weeks back, so our instinct went straight to infrastructure rather than a recent deploy.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: That's a really common failure mode in incident response, anchoring on the most recent similar incident even if it's unrelated.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Yeah, in hindsight the deploy timeline lined up almost exactly with when errors started, we should have checked recent deploys first.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Let's talk impact. How many customers actually noticed?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: We had eleven support tickets overnight and this morning specifically about missing data or gaps in their funnels for that time window.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: Any of our bigger accounts affected?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: BrightLoop was one of them actually, they noticed a gap in their overnight campaign tracking data.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Given everything going on with BrightLoop already, that's not great timing.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Agreed, I feel pretty bad about that honestly given they're already frustrated with funnel performance.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Not blaming anyone here, mistakes happen, we're here to fix the process. What about data loss, did any events get permanently dropped or just delayed?

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Good news there, nothing was permanently lost. Rejected events went to a dead letter queue instead of being discarded, so we were able to replay all of them once the hotfix went out.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Replay finished around one AM, so by the time customers woke up this morning, their data was actually complete, just delayed by a few hours.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: That's a relief, could have been a lot worse.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Agreed, good that the dead letter queue caught it. Okay, let's get into what we're actually changing so this doesn't happen again.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: First thing, I want to establish a hard rule, any schema change that adds a required field must ship as optional first, with a follow up deploy making it required only after we confirm the backlog is drained.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: I like that as a policy, can we put that in our deployment checklist formally, not just tribal knowledge?

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Yes, I'll write that up and add it to the checklist doc this week.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Second thing, from the response side, we should have checked recent deploys within the first five minutes, not after twenty. I want to add a deploy timeline widget directly into our incident dashboard so it's the first thing anyone sees.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: That's a good idea, how much work is that?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Pretty small, maybe a day, it's just surfacing data we already have in a more visible place.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: Let's prioritize that this week given how directly it would have shortened this incident.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Agreed, I'll have it done by Friday.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Third thing, we should add a specific alert for validation rejection rate on ingestion, not just general error rate. We would have caught this within a minute or two instead of waiting for the broader error rate alert to fire.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Do that too, seems like a quick win.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: I'll add that alert this week as well, shouldn't take more than a couple hours.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: What about customer communication, did we proactively notify anyone or did they all come to us?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: All eleven tickets came from customers noticing on their own, we didn't send anything proactive since we didn't fully understand scope until it was basically resolved.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: Should we have a status page update threshold, like anything over ten minutes of degraded service triggers an automatic post?

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: I think yes, that's overdue honestly, we've talked about a status page for a while.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: I can own setting that up, low effort using an existing status page tool, I'd guess half a day of work.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Let's do it, and specifically loop in Aisha so customer success can proactively reach out to affected accounts like BrightLoop next time, even before a fix is in place. Let's also talk about severity classification for a second. Was this correctly classified as our highest severity level, or did it take too long to escalate internally?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: It was classified correctly once I understood scope, but I think I sat on it as a medium severity issue for maybe three or four minutes longer than I should have, right around the ten twenty two mark when it jumped to forty three percent.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: What made you hesitate on escalating faster?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Honestly just wanting to confirm it wasn't a blip before waking people up at ten PM. In hindsight, given how fast it was climbing, I should have paged immediately rather than waiting to confirm the trend.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: That's a fair instinct generally, but I think the lesson here is any error rate climbing that fast, doubling within a couple minutes, should trigger immediate escalation regardless of confirmation.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Could we bake that into the alerting rule itself, like a rate of change trigger rather than just an absolute threshold?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: That's a good idea actually, right now our alert is just a static threshold at five percent error rate. A rate of change trigger would catch something like this even earlier, potentially before it crosses the static threshold at all.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: How much work would a rate of change alert be to build?

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: More involved than the other items, maybe three or four days, since it needs a rolling window calculation rather than a simple point in time check.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Let's scope that properly rather than rush it, put it on next sprint's planning rather than trying to squeeze it in this week with everything else.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Agreed, that feels like the right pace for something that needs to be built carefully rather than hotfixed.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: Good, let's make sure it doesn't get lost though, I'll add it to next sprint's backlog myself so it doesn't rely on anyone remembering this conversation.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: That would have helped a lot here honestly, BrightLoop finding out from us rather than noticing themselves would have landed very differently given everything else going on.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: Agreed. Let's make sure Aisha gets looped into future incident response for major accounts specifically.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: Noted, I'll talk to Aisha separately about being on the notification list for major account impact.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: Alright, let's recap the action items. Kenji adds the required field migration policy to the deployment checklist, adds the validation rejection alert, and we already know the hotfix is stable. Dimitri builds the deploy timeline widget and sets up the status page, both by Friday.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: That's right.

segments.speaker: Tom Becker
segments.text: And I'll follow up with Aisha on incident notification process for major accounts. I think that covers it, thanks everyone for the honest retro, this was a good one despite the rough night.

segments.speaker: Kenji Watanabe
segments.text: Thanks, and sorry again for six minutes of half asleep panic.

segments.speaker: Dimitri Petrov
segments.text: Happens to all of us, you handled it well once you were up.

segments.speaker: Marcus Johnson
segments.text: Agreed, good work getting it resolved as fast as you did. Thanks everyone.

summary.overview:
The team reviewed a full outage of the event ingestion pipeline lasting roughly 35 minutes (with 16 minutes of degraded service before it), caused by a schema migration that added a required field without backward compatibility for a backlog of queued events in the old format. Error rates climbed from 0.1% to a peak of 100% between 10:14 PM and 10:30 PM before Kenji identified the root cause and shipped a one-line hotfix at 11:02 PM, restoring normal service by 11:10 PM. Initial troubleshooting was slowed by anchoring on a recent, unrelated staging disk space issue instead of checking recent deploys first.

No data was permanently lost since rejected events were captured in a dead letter queue and fully replayed by 1 AM, though eleven customers, including BrightLoop Retail, noticed gaps in their overnight data and filed support tickets. The team acknowledged the timing was especially unfortunate given BrightLoop's existing frustration with Funnel Builder performance.

Follow-up actions include a formal deployment checklist rule requiring new required fields to ship as optional first, a deploy timeline widget on the incident dashboard, a dedicated validation rejection rate alert, and a status page with an automatic posting threshold. The team also discussed a roughly three to four minute escalation delay while confirming the trend before paging, and agreed a future rate-of-change based alert (rather than a static threshold) would catch a similar spike earlier; Marcus will add that to next sprint's backlog. Tom will also follow up with Aisha about looping customer success into incident response for major accounts going forward.
